note: quince#348. `issue-new` re-fired on EVERY tick, forever, for every issue above the highwater — so a watch exited on tick 1 on every arm and could never reach a quiet state. Measured on the implementer box: three consecutive ticks, seconds apart, no forge activity between them, eight identical `issue-new` lines each time, and `highwater` unchanged at 309 while `last_tick` advanced. THE CAUSE IS IN THE WRITE-BACK, NOT IN THE DIFF. `step()` builds `$decl` as the previous issue block minus `items` (forge-watch:359) — which carries the previous `open_seen` and `scan_limit` as well as the declared set — and the persist then did `.issues = ($decl + {items: …})`, restoring the OLD scan over the fresh one. The highwater line immediately below computes `max($decl.highwater, .issues.open_seen)`, and by then `.issues.open_seen` IS the old list, so it could only ever return what it already was. The diff that EMITS the events reads `$_now.issues.open_seen` and was always correct: the tool noticed the new issues and then failed to remember it had. WHY 63 FIXTURES PASSED ON THE BROKEN CODE, which is the reason this file is a `sequence` and not a pair: every `issue-new` fixture was a single before/after step, and one step cannot observe that the second step repeats itself. A pair fixture asserts what a tick EMITS; only a sequence asserts what the tick LEAVES BEHIND, and the defect lived entirely in what was left behind. TICK 0 IS THE CONTROL AND TICK 1 IS THE CLAIM: 340 and 335 are above the highwater of 330 and are news exactly once; 322 is below it and is never news; the second tick sees the identical scan and must be SILENT. Against the broken write-back, tick 1 emits the same two lines again and this fixture fails on both the events and the state predicate.

steps.label: two issues above the highwater are news, once
the identical scan, one tick later, is SILENT
a genuinely new issue is still news after convergence
